drills.q: You need all-pairs shortest paths on a sparse graph (V=10,000, E=30,000) that may contain negative edges but no negative cycles. Which algorithm and why?
drills.a: Johnson's algorithm, O(VE + V^2 log V) ~ 1.3*10^9 operations, vs Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) ~ 10^12 -- three orders of magnitude faster on this sparse graph.

drills.q: Derive why w'(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v) is always non-negative after Bellman-Ford computes h from a virtual source (assuming no negative cycle).
drills.a: Bellman-Ford's convergence guarantees h(v) <= h(u) + w(u,v) for every edge (otherwise it would still be relaxable). Rearranging: w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v) >= 0.

drills.q: After running Dijkstra on Johnson's reweighted graph, how do you recover the real shortest distance between u and v, and why does this work?
drills.a: dist(u,v) = dist'(u,v) - h(u) + h(v). It works because the reweighted cost of any path telescopes to the real cost plus the constant h(u)-h(v), which is the same shift for every path between the same two endpoints, so it doesn't change which path is shortest.

drills.q: You want to know if ANY arbitrage cycle exists across all currency pairs (not starting from one specific currency). Why does a virtual source matter here instead of picking one arbitrary starting currency?
drills.a: An arbitrary real currency node might not reach every other node (one-way convertibility or disconnected subgraphs), silently missing an arbitrage cycle unreachable from it. A virtual source connects to every currency directly, guaranteeing full reachability so Bellman-Ford's negative-cycle check covers the whole graph.

drills.q: Compare the total cost of Johnson's algorithm to running Bellman-Ford from every vertex directly (no reweighting). What does the reweighting step actually buy you?
drills.a: Bellman-Ford from every vertex: O(V * VE) = O(V^2 E). Johnson's: O(VE + V^2 log V). The reweighting substitutes V cheap Dijkstra runs for V expensive Bellman-Ford runs, paying the Bellman-Ford cost only once (for potentials) instead of V times.

drills.q: Your all-pairs shortest path system on a 500,000-node sparse graph needs repeated point-to-point queries, and even Johnson's O(V^2) output storage is too much memory. What's the production escalation beyond Johnson's algorithm?
drills.a: Contraction hierarchies or hub labeling: heavier one-time preprocessing that answers individual point-to-point queries in near-constant to logarithmic time without ever materializing the full O(V^2) distance matrix.
